# 01 — Text-to-image: building the visual reference system

The image stage produced three kinds of references: empty photographic locations, multi-view character sheets, and object references. The location images described the film's world; the character sheets protected identity from shot to shot; the object references protected the geometry of the four-wheel cart and the printed cardboard package. These were production inputs, not substitutes for continuity checks in moving images.

## Character sheets

The original script contains English Midjourney-style character-sheet prompts for the grandmother, fruit-shop owner, and recycling-station worker. The wording below is a cleaned English presentation of that source. The source used a 16:9 sheet; the eventual moving footage used a 4:3 frame. The sheet aspect ratio was therefore a reference-layout choice, not the film's output ratio.

**Grandmother — reference:** character1.png

> Photographic character reference sheet for an older Hong Kong Cantonese woman who collects discarded cardboard. Show consistent front, side, back, face close-up, and high-angle views on a neutral light-grey background. Severe, permanent forward bend; weathered skin; high cheekbones; grey-streaked hair tied low and untidily; a faded dark floral blouse, worn apron with a zip pocket, loose trousers, and old oversized clogs. Include small detail studies of hair, hands, cloth, and footwear. Natural light, restrained expression, real skin texture, no illustration or 3D mannequin.

**Fruit-shop owner — reference:** character2.png

> Photographic multi-view reference sheet of a Hong Kong neighbourhood fruit-shop owner in his forties. Consistent front, side, back, and face views on a neutral background. Sturdy working build, slightly sun-tanned skin, short hair, faded cotton polo shirt, market apron, and a towel over one shoulder. Friendly but practical presence. Include close studies of face, hands, clothing and apron. Documentary realism, natural imperfections, no illustration or 3D appearance.

**Recycling-station worker — reference:** character3.png

> Photographic multi-view reference sheet of a young Hong Kong recycling-station worker in his twenties. Thin working build, casually slouched posture, slightly unkempt short hair, faded T-shirt, cargo shorts, and worn trainers. Show the same face and clothing in front, side, back, and close-up views. Neutral light-grey studio background; natural skin and fabric texture; no stylised rendering.

**Finding.** The side view mattered most for the grandmother: “elderly woman” alone did not preserve her long-standing bent posture. The sheets kept identity and clothing stable, while the video prompt still had to describe weight transfer and short steps so the posture did not become a rigid model pose.

## Object sheets and material continuity

- Empty cart, four-view reference: rusted tubular frame, four wheels, open metal-mesh platform, and handle geometry.
- Loaded cart reference: the direction and height of many accumulated flattened boxes.
- Printed package reference: white coated board with a large printed face. It was treated as a small package among ordinary discarded boxes, rather than a huge freestanding celebrity poster.

The printed face needed to occupy a substantial area of the main panel so that folding the board through its centre would visibly halve the face. In the overhead location plate, the package was scaled to neighbouring waste cartons and given dirt and wear so it belonged to the pile. The cart's base was corrected from a solid slab to open metal mesh; the load was corrected from a single low layer to a substantial, compressed stack. The working S4 reference is the revised overhead plate.

## Scene-plate prompt family

The following are English portfolio versions of the location prompts. They describe the final spatial brief; they are not claims that a single text-only pass created every plate. Several images were revised against an existing scene and Blender camera. A location plate generally excluded the grandmother and cart so Seedance could place them from separate references.

### A. Old Hong Kong street and intersection — S1, S2, S8, S16

> Wide 4:3 documentary photograph of an older Hong Kong district: dense mid-rise residential façades, ageing air conditioners, pipes, shop signs, pedestrian rails, road markings, and an overcast sky. Natural grey-green colour, deep focus, imperfect surfaces and believable street scale. Reserve a continuous pedestrian route and a separate vehicle lane. Keep the camera fixed at human height, with clear foreground, middle ground, and distant architecture. No staged portrait, no new central subject, no glossy cinematic lighting.

For S8 and S16, the intersection plate had to support very small people in a broad street view. Scale was repeatedly corrected by using road position and projected figure height rather than writing only “make the grandmother smaller.” The S16 prompt eventually used an approximately one-tenth-frame figure height as a compositional anchor. See S8 and S16.

### B. Fruit-shop slope — S3, S5, S13, S14

> Full-width, near-frontal 4:3 photograph of an old Hong Kong fruit shop with a muted red-edged canvas awning, lit fruit display, adjoining shutters, roadside railing, reused plastic crates and finite piles of flattened cardboard. The street rises physically from screen left to screen right by approximately fifteen degrees: curb, yellow lines, pavement and railing rise together. Buildings, window jambs and rail posts remain upright; floor lines remain level. Desaturated overcast light, worn surfaces and damp asphalt. Preserve a usable path between the piles and railing. Empty location plate: no grandmother or cart.

The source screenplay originally described a thirty-degree optical illusion. The production changed that into a real, approximately fifteen-degree uphill street. A Blender camera helped distinguish an actual slope from a rotated photograph. The S3 plate revision record documents the geometry correction. For the return, the shop plate kept the same world while emptying the cardboard area and placing the owner outside, sweeping. The brief retained daytime overcast brightness instead of turning the scene into night.

### C. Overhead cardboard and cart — S4

> True vertical overhead photograph of the same shop-side pavement. Open-mesh rusted four-wheel handcart parallel to the railing, carrying an accumulated stack of compressed cardboard. Nearby waste pile contains one ordinary-size white coated printed food package with a large face image and a central fold path. The board is weathered and partly surrounded by other waste, yet its face remains legible. Preserve exact ground, railing, fixed piles, cart proportions, and road orientation. Leave clear separation between bodies and objects; no people in the empty plate.

This plate underwent several revisions: first the printed board was too conspicuous, then its white material drifted toward brown kraft paper, and the cart load was too shallow. The final version restarted from an earlier base plate to stop background drift. See S4 image records.

### D. Low cart-side street — S6

> Low, close, forward cart-side view up a wet Hong Kong slope. Weathered roadside barrier recedes beside old apartment façades; the background is arranged for forward motion parallax. Overcast grey-green documentary light, realistic rain-softened distance and road texture. Keep a credible open space for the grandmother and cart in the foreground. Empty plate: no person, no cart, no model shading.

The camera reference came from a white-model cart-side test, but the location plate needed to remain photographic. See the clean S6 location plate.

### E. Cargo-level intersection — S7

> Ground-skimming 4:3 view of a Hong Kong intersection from the approximate height of a cardboard load. Road markings, curb edge and old buildings establish a continuous route from pedestrian pavement into the carriageway. Keep the roadway open for a slow forward movement and later right turn. Overcast light and realistic road depth. No people, cart, or vehicle in the clean plate; the approaching van is introduced later in the video action.

The second view was revised so the roadside railing did not reappear after the cart had left the pedestrian route. The two location references are S7-A and S7-B.

### F. Recycling-station interior and exterior — S9, S10, S11

> Documentary photograph from inside a small recycling depot toward a daylight opening: damp concrete floor, left-hand stored cardboard bales and floor scale, right-hand fan and plastic chair, crates, dim fluorescents, and rain-muted street beyond. Preserve a genuinely clear entrance for a loaded cart. No people in the location plate.

For S10, the camera changed to a **low but perfectly vertical overhead view**: the iron scale and wet cardboard sit on one part of the floor; the empty cart rests apart from them; a clear visible gap prevents the stored left-hand pile from merging with the scale load. For S11, an exterior plate showed the depot opening between bales and stacked cartons. References: S9, S10, S11.

### G. Empty-cart POV and final overhead — S12, S15

> S12: very low road-level view up a narrow canyon of ageing Hong Kong apartment blocks, with empty foreground space for a cart-mounted reverse-facing camera. Natural overcast perspective, textured asphalt and muted distance; no person or cart in the clean plate.

> S15: strict vertical overhead location photograph. A weathered red canvas awning occupies the left side, narrow pavement and railing run beside it, and damp road fills the right. Clear space for the cart to move downward through the frame. The awning should conceal most of the shopkeeper when the figures are later added.

References: S12 and S15.

**Overall finding.** Text-to-image was strongest at supplying material, mood, and architectural identity. It was least reliable when asked to preserve precise object counts, cart structure, or geometry across repeated edits. Those requirements moved into a reference hierarchy and Blender layout, while the scene image remained an appearance anchor.

# 02 — Designing text prompts for controllable shots

The writing task was less about finding evocative adjectives than about assigning each reference a job. In this project, an image could establish a street and its lighting, a character sheet could establish identity, and a Blender video could establish movement. When all of them were treated as equally authoritative for every property, the generated shots drifted in scale, cast, cargo, and weather.

## Prompt hierarchy

The working prompt structure became:

1. **Output contract:** duration, 4:3 frame, fixed or mounted camera, uninterrupted time, photorealism.
2. **Reference roles:** which uploaded image controls geography, which controls each face, which controls cart structure, and which video controls only blocking.
3. **Opening inventory:** where each person and object starts, what is loaded on the cart, what stays fixed in the background.
4. **Spatial route:** screen direction, road or pavement layer, relation to the railing, and physically reachable path.
5. **One main action:** contact, force, transfer, release, and resulting state where necessary.
6. **Speech and sound:** speaker, language, approximate cue, and environmental sound below dialogue.
7. **Continuity checks:** no sudden crop, unwanted zoom, teleportation, extra cardboard, or background replacement.

The same order is reflected in the shot-by-shot English prompts. Their wording has been edited for portfolio readability. The original saved Chinese examples are available in S3, S4, S5, and selected later Blender-linked prompts.

## Reference roles in practice

| Input | Allowed to determine | Explicitly prevented from determining |
|---|---|---|
| Empty scene plate | Architecture, weather, framing, fixed props, colour | Character identity or how an actor moves |
| Character sheet | Face, age, hair, clothes, characteristic posture | Studio background, portrait camera, scene lighting |
| Cart and package sheets | Wheel count, mesh platform, handles, board material, scale | Extra cargo or a new viewpoint |
| Blender animation | Starting positions, trajectory, camera and action timing | Final human skin, clothing, facial performance, grey-model look |
| Previous clip's final frame | Local continuity at the start of a new shot | A forced ending or abrupt mid-shot layout change |

This hierarchy evolved after two opposite failures. With only start and end frames, the model sometimes “solved” the transition by adding cardboard or jumping directly to the target frame. With a white-model video weighted too heavily, it sometimes copied model-like people. The later workflow used the previous video frame for immediate continuity and Blender for the route, while photographic references supplied appearance.

## Translating action into physical cause and effect

S3 is the clearest example. “She throws cardboard onto the cart” left too much freedom: the pile could refill, and new sheets could appear near the cart. The revised instruction tracked **one existing bundle** from the top of the crate stack, through her hands, to the cart. The original pile needed a visible gap; the cart gained only the corresponding volume. A short impact and cart vibration replaced a large theatrical toss.

S4 used the same logic for a fold: there was only one white printed board, it stayed attached along its fold line, and the crease passed through the face. A request for “a folded box” alone tended to produce an intermediate bent sheet rather than a complete half-face silhouette, so the desired physical end state also received its own still reference.

S5 was simplified after repeated jump cuts. The first versions included stepping on cardboard, tying rope, loading, and leaving inside one short shot. The later version reduced the action to a single continuous push of an already loaded cart. Fixed piles and a small bin were named as immobile objects so the model would not move or invent them while the cart departed.

## Camera and scale as measurable instructions

“Wide shot” was not sufficient. The model repeatedly enlarged the grandmother or cropped the shop to make hand actions legible. The prompts therefore described stable screen anchors: the whole awning and road remain visible; the person stands in a middle-ground strip; the cart stays attached to her; buildings and railing keep their initial pixel positions. S16 added a projected figure height of roughly one tenth of the frame after earlier renders made her too large in the intersection.

The model also needed an explicit distinction between **moving camera** and **moving subject**. S6 follows beside the cart at a low angle, S7 moves with the cardboard load, and S3/S5/S13/S14 remain locked on a tripod. Words such as “cinematic movement” were avoided because they often invited a zoom, pan, or fresh crop.

## Prompt compression and dialogue

Longer prompts were useful when the core uncertainty was spatial, such as which side of a railing the cart occupied. They were counterproductive when a distant action was described like a close-up. S11's handoff was initially overexplained, and the generated image repeatedly cropped in to show the money and paper. The sequence was split into payment, retrieval, and departure; the retrieval became a broad gesture in a fixed exterior frame. Dialogue cues were tied to an observable action, for example the worker calls out when the cart crosses the threshold, rather than to an arbitrary last second.

The Cantonese lines were kept in Chinese in production prompts even when the surrounding instruction was rewritten in English. A portfolio translation can describe their meaning, but exact spoken wording is part of the sound design. The complete source script is here.

## Weather and finishing

Weather became a continuity issue of its own. Negative wording such as “no rain” did not reliably remove rain already present in a video reference; the model still inherited streaks and wet sound. The later process separated small-rain atmosphere from camera, performance, and colour, and experimented with post-production rain reduction. These are production findings, not evidence that a prompt alone can erase baked-in pixels. See the local rain-repair tests and shot-specific edits.

**Takeaway:** the most effective prompt described a constrained, filmable event. It named the start state, the permitted change, and the end state, while keeping camera and background independent of the action.

# 03 — Blender as a spatial rehearsal tool

Blender was used to answer questions that text prompts and image references could not answer precisely: Where is the camera? How large is the grandmother in frame? Is the cart in front of her? Can the cart pass the door? Does a board intersect her head when opened? The grey or white-model renders were **previsualisation**, not final imagery. Seedance was instructed to convert those routes into natural human performance using the photographic character sheets.

## Three useful outputs

**A camera and scale check.** The model fixed a camera, rough architecture, a human proxy, and a cart proxy. This exposed composition errors before generation. For example, S3's uphill Blender animation tested a real rising street while keeping shop façades vertical; S16's final white blocking tested a much smaller walker against a wide intersection.

**A movement guide.** A short render gave the generator a route, turning radius, and camera relationship without giving it final materials. S7's continuous cargo POV separated straight movement out of the pedestrian area from a subsequent slow right turn. S6's low front follow protected the cart-mounted angle and same-direction camera travel.

**A clearance test.** Doorways, handcart frames, fixed stacks, scales, and railings were treated as geometry rather than descriptive background. Review scripts and notes in S9, S10, S11, and S14 record these checks. They catch obvious intersections in the proxy scene; they do not certify that a generated video will never clip.

## How the blocking evolved

| Storyboard area | Blender question | Working answer / revision |
|---|---|---|
| S1–S2 | How small should the grandmother and cart read against traffic and buildings? | Early browser/white-model tests informed the wide-framing language; the final generated clips remained independent of the proxy look. |
| S3 | Is the street physically uphill or merely a rotated photograph? | Rebuilt the slope at approximately 15° while keeping façades, windows, and posts upright. S3 v02. |
| S4 | Can hands and folded board fit in a true overhead composition? | Vertical overhead cart/pavement layout, later revised to leave clear object separation. S4 v03. |
| S5 | Does the departing cart have a clear continuous route? | Reused S3's fixed geography and reduced the action to forward travel instead of compressing loading, stepping, tying, and departure into one shot. |
| S6 | What does a cart-side low follow shot actually see? | Moved the camera with the cart and tested low/front-side versions before using a photographic scene plate. S6 v03. |
| S7 | Can a heavy cart leave the pedestrian route and turn without pivoting in place? | Integrated position from heading, split straight exit and slow turn, changed the second turn from left to right, and removed the railing from the second view. S7 v02. |
| S8 | How far away are the grandmother and van, and who is nearer the building? | Pushed both into the distance, positioned the van deeper than the grandmother, and kept her route toward the left street rather than straight across the foreground. S8 v04. |
| S9 | Can the full cart enter the depot without crossing the worker or the scale? | Modelled a real entrance, worker's small yielding step, and loaded-cart path from the street. S9 v01. |
| S10 | Is the overhead camera lower yet still truly vertical? | Reworked the camera through several versions; preserved a gap between stored paper and scale load. S10 v04. |
| S11 | Which cart is hers, where is its handle, and which direction does she leave? | Split the interaction into payment, retrieval, and departure. Corrected the handle to screen left and the exit to screen left. The front scale pile remains separate from her cart farther inside. S11 C v08. |
| S12 | Does a rear-facing camera on an almost empty cart still show the grandmother and receding city? | Attached a low camera to the cart and tested bounce and visible handle/feet. S12 v01. |
| S13 | Is the returning grandmother outside the railing and behind the cart? | Reversed travel direction, kept her on the road side, and staged the owner sweeping before he notices her. S13 v02. |
| S14 | Can she open the board while the cart stays still, and can the bag reach its handle? | Tested board-to-head clearance, bag passage above the railing, and a shorter complete action of about 15 seconds. S14 v03. |
| S15 | Does the red awning hide most of the owner from directly above? | Locked a vertical camera while the cart and mostly hidden grandmother move down-frame. S15 v01. |
| S16 | Does the reverse-direction walk retain human-scale proportions and hand contact? | Rebuilt a clean white blocking shot with a smaller silhouette: left hand holds the board, right hand remains on the cart, fruit bag at her left-side handle. S16 v05. |

## What Blender did not solve

The models could establish plausible routes and check proxy collisions, but they could not generate the final face, wet cloth, Cantonese speech, or the subtle strain of an older person walking. A geometry-perfect turn could still become a jump cut or a car U-turn in Seedance. The generator also sometimes enlarged the subject to show an action despite correct white-model scale. The revised prompt therefore repeated the *relationship* between actor, cart, railing, and fixed camera while telling the model to use real skin and natural body mechanics.

The transferable technique is to model the **variables that need exact answers**. Here they were camera placement, projected size, spatial layer, turning arc, door clearance, and prop ownership. Materials and emotional performance remained separate production tasks.

# 04 — Seedance production: prompts, visible results, and findings

This shotbook presents the complete sixteen-shot storyboard in English. Each **Production prompt** is a concise, reusable English reconstruction of the shot's working instructions. It is **not** a verbatim transcript of every original Chinese submission. Surviving original drafts are collected in the prompt archive below. **Observed result** describes an available export or sampled frame, and **Finding / revision** records an issue discovered during production and the change made in response. The project used 4:3 photorealistic video, restrained grey-green light, natural Cantonese dialogue when scripted, and a mostly fixed-camera visual grammar.

The local contact sheet shows one sampled frame from each available export. S7 has two passages. `S13.mp4` and `S13-2.mp4` are different working segments; `S14.mp4` contains a longer combined interaction. File names alone should not be read as a locked final edit list.

## S1 — The collector enters the city

Still · Working export · Surviving Chinese prompt

**Production prompt.** A fixed 4:3 Hong Kong street wide shot. The grandmother, permanently bent at the waist, slowly pushes a single rusted four-wheel open-mesh cart through a middle-ground pedestrian route while traffic moves much faster in a distinct foreground lane. Match her face and clothes to the character sheet and the cart's structure to its object sheet; use real people and worn street materials, never grey-model shading. Keep her small relative to the architecture and vehicles. Maintain the entire original frame, natural road noise and cart rattle, no close-up or music.

**Observed result.** The sampled frame places her behind a dark metal grid, producing a strong sense of separation from the city. **Finding / revision.** Wide framing helped the social contrast, but spatial depth had to be written explicitly: traffic, pavement, person, and cart must occupy different layers. “Small person” alone did not control perspective or cart placement.

## S2 — Waiting at the intersection

Still · Working export · Surviving Chinese prompt

**Production prompt.** Fixed low-angle 4:3 view of a broad Hong Kong junction framed by old residential buildings. Keep the grandmother and one cart in the lower part of the image at a credible distance; she pauses for a signal, then starts again. Her bent torso and straight lower legs form a graphic folded shape against the upright city. Only restrained weight shifts and breathing during the wait. Keep buildings stable, preserve road scale, and use crossing beeps and street sound without added score.

**Observed result.** The working frame shows a very small figure and cart against the large empty junction. **Finding / revision.** That scale later became a continuity benchmark for S16. The same location plate could be reused, but its geometry did not by itself specify which direction the returning cart should travel.

## S3 — One bundle of cardboard

Still · Working export · Refined working export · Saved prompt

**Production prompt.** Fixed distant side view of the fruit shop on a real street rising approximately fifteen degrees toward screen right. Buildings and rail posts stay upright. The grandmother and empty cart are on the shop-side pavement behind the railing. She touches, grips, lifts, and transfers **one existing bundle** of flattened cardboard from the crate-top pile into the cart. The source pile keeps a visible gap and the cart gains that same bundle; no extra paper appears. She stays hunched and moves with believable weight. The shopkeeper and a few customers continue quiet, separated activity around the fruit display, not all in the doorway. One continuous camera and action; no zoom for the hand movement.

**Observed result.** The shop geography and steep pavement line are legible in the wide frame. **Finding / revision.** The initial 30° tilted-building concept became a real 15° uphill street after Blender calibration. Later prompts moved from a vague “throw cardboard” command to a tracked object transfer. The shop background also needed more people and spacing; “one customer in the shop” concentrated all activity in a small doorway.

## S4 — Folding the printed board

Still · Working export · Saved prompt

**Production prompt.** True vertical overhead fixed shot, matched to the fruit-shop pavement, railing, and cart. A single small white coated printed carton lies among similarly sized discarded boxes. Its portrait occupies most of the visible face and its fold line crosses the face. The grandmother's weathered hands take this one carton and fold it completely in half along the crease: one continuous physical sheet, the printed face reduced to one visible half. Her motion is slow and effortful, not the sharp robotic action of a pose test. The cart has an open metal-mesh base and a substantial stack of compressed cardboard aligned lengthwise. Neither body, paper, cart nor railing intersects.

**Observed result.** The overhead frame clearly shows the portrait-bearing sheet near the cart. **Finding / revision.** Several image versions made the package too large or changed its white coated stock into brown board. An explicit half-face reference was needed because “fold in half” often produced only a partly bent sheet. The cart load was corrected from a loose shallow layer to an accumulated stack.

## S5 — Leaving the fruit shop

Still · Working export · Saved later prompt

**Production prompt.** Continue the same fixed S3 composition and right-rising pavement. The grandmother already has the accumulated cardboard on one rusted cart. She stands behind its handle and pushes slowly toward screen right along the shop-side pavement, without stopping, loading more paper, stepping on it, or tying rope. The cargo remains inside the cart frame and moves as a single assembly with the wheels; no sheets appear in front of or behind her. The remaining stack, fruit display, small grey-blue bin, shopkeeper and customers are fixed background; the people continue subtle conversation. Leave the frame by crossing its right boundary naturally, cart first, then grandmother. Camera, crop and exposure remain unchanged.

**Observed result.** A wide shop view remains while the cart moves along the railing. **Finding / revision.** Combining loading, stepping, tying and departure in seven seconds produced jump cuts. Start/end-frame tests also invented cardboard to bridge two states. The final instruction kept one observable action and used an asset-reference workflow rather than demanding a forced end frame.

## S6 — Weight on the slope

Still · Working export · Blender movement test

**Production prompt.** An eight-second low camera travels beside the cart's front side at the grandmother's pace, looking slightly up across the heavy bundle toward her upper body. The cart jolts on the incline but advances continuously. She stays bent, presses her weight into the handle, and takes short hard steps; skin, clothing and breathing remain human and irregular. Old Hong Kong façades and railing slide backward through shallow rain haze while the cart and grandmother stay in a stable relative position. The white-model clip provides only camera path and timing; the character, cart and location references provide photographic appearance. No mechanical puppet movements, extra cargo or camera cuts.

**Observed result.** The available frame shows the cardboard close to camera and the grandmother straining behind the handle. **Finding / revision.** A purely empty scene image could not convey the mounted viewpoint. Low-front Blender blocking clarified what occupies foreground and how the camera follows without changing the cart/person relationship.

## S7 — Cargo POV, pavement exit and right turn

Straight-exit still · Straight-exit export · Right-turn still · Second export · Blender route

**Production prompt, passage A.** The camera is attached low to the load, looking forward from the cart. In one uninterrupted six-second movement it rolls straight off the pedestrian route toward the roadway. The visible board edge and road texture advance together; the camera does not swing, the route does not turn, and the curb is crossed only once. Keep a continuous world with believable frame-to-frame displacement.

**Production prompt, passage B.** Continue from passage A's last position. The heavy cart advances while making a slow right turn into the road; rotation follows the path rather than pivoting in place. The rail is now behind camera and absent from the new view. A business van approaches in the roadway, brakes close enough to create tension, honks impatiently, then steers around the cart by changing lane and passes; it does not perform a U-turn. Keep the van's single identity, size and route consistent. No cut, teleport, duplicate cart or sudden background shift.

**Observed result.** The first working frame reaches an exposed roadway; the second puts an approaching van directly ahead. **Finding / revision.** A first/last-frame-only attempt weakened the sense that the camera was attached to a cart and produced mid-shot spatial jumps. The route was split into straight exit and turn. A “turning vehicle” instruction had to become a specific lane-change path so the van did not turn around in place.

## S8 — A distant protest

Still · Working export · Saved prompt

**Production prompt.** Locked 4:3 wide view of a large junction. The grandmother and cart begin far from camera, near the base of the central building, and head toward the street on the left side of the composition. The departing van is also distant, in a deeper traffic layer closer to the building, so it does not cover her. The van moves away to screen right; she briefly pauses without straightening and calls after it in Cantonese: “呠咩呠啊，我都係四個轆㗎！” She then resumes pushing. No foreground enlargement, no van rubber-banding, no extra traffic conflict or camera follow.

**Observed result.** Both figures are small against the junction and its central building. **Finding / revision.** Earlier attempts placed the grandmother and van near the lens and sent her laterally across the frame instead of toward the left street. The revision separated their depth planes and named the destination street, not just “move left.”

## S9 — Entering the recycling depot

Still · Working export · Longer variant · Blender blocking

**Production prompt.** Fixed camera inside the dim recycling depot, looking out through the existing entrance to the wet street. The cardboard load appears in the opening first, followed by the same cart and hunched grandmother as she turns carefully inside. Keep the stack at its established height; it must not grow into a tower. The worker, initially seated near the fan and phone, notices the wheel noise, stands and makes room at the doorway. He says in natural Cantonese, “阿婆，落咁大雨都過嚟啊。推埋嚟過磅啦。” Keep the doorway, left stored pile, floor scale, fan and chair where the scene plate places them. No camera move or obstruction crossing.

**Observed result.** The interior view shows the worker standing to one side while the grandmother approaches through the door. **Finding / revision.** The first generated cart carried paper far higher than in previous shots. Later instructions fixed the top of the load below a clear visual height and let the entry unfold more slowly in a longer clip.

## S10 — The weight and the refusal

Still · Working export · Saved prompt

**Production prompt.** Inside the same depot, use a lower ceiling-lamp camera but point it exactly vertically downward throughout. A wide low pile of water-softened ordinary cardboard lies on the black iron scale; the grandmother's open-mesh cart, now mostly empty, remains separately at lower right. There is a visible strip of floor between the scale load and stored paper at upper left. She places the only folded white printed board, with half a face visible, on top. The worker approaches and lightly nudges the bottom edge of the wet paper once with his shoe. He objects in Cantonese that the company will not accept paper soaked with water. She glances at the scale without standing upright and replies that the rule seems to have changed only after she placed it there. Maintain one board and one existing paper load; no piles merge or grow.

**Observed result.** The sampled overhead frame separates the printed top board, worker, grandmother, stored paper and cart. **Finding / revision.** The camera initially became a slanted overhead view; the corrected version lowered the camera while preserving a true 90° downward axis. The upper-left stored pile also needed a clear gap to stop it visually intersecting the scale pile. A softer scene plate helped avoid over-sharpened texture.

## S11 — Payment, retrieval, and departure

Still · Combined working export · A/B/C Blender sequence · Final exit blocking

**Production prompt A: payment.** Fixed exterior full façade of the recycling station. Keep both characters and the grandmother's own open-mesh cart inside the doorway, at a small realistic scale. The wet paper on the front floor scale is a separate pile, not her cart. The worker offers half price; she accepts the money with a restrained gesture and calls him stingy. The whole awning, façade, left bales, right carton stacks and foreground road remain in frame. Do not zoom into the hands.

**Production prompt B: retrieval.** Continue from A's exact last frame. Without changing camera or position, the grandmother makes a small readable movement to reclaim the one folded printed board and place it on her cart farther inside. The action needs only to read in the wide shot; do not invent a hand close-up, new cardboard load, or new camera angle. The worker stays near the entrance.

**Production prompt C: exit.** Continue from B's final arrangement. The grandmother reaches the handle on the cart's screen-left side and pushes it out of the depot. The worker yields a small step and stays inside. Her cart passes the threshold and proceeds toward screen left; the front scale and soaked paper never move. As she has just stepped outside, the worker calls after her in Cantonese, “喂！？你執紙皮都咁計較㗎。” She does not speak, stop or look back. Fixed full façade and one continuous exit.

**Observed result.** The available combined export shows the exterior depot with the figures small inside the opening. **Finding / revision.** This was the most iterative shot. A detailed description of receiving banknotes triggered unwanted crops and zooms; splitting the scene into A/B/C and making B a broad gesture helped protect the wide camera. The cart was first confused with the wet paper in front, its handle side was corrected, and the exit route changed to screen left. The assembled clip still received separate seam alignment and quality-matching work; those processes are documented in S11 repair notes.

## S12 — The nearly empty cart looks backward

Still · Working export · Saved prompt

**Production prompt.** A camera rigidly attached low to the nearly empty cart's platform faces back and upward toward the grandmother. Only a folded printed board remains; no heavy paper load returns. The cart rattles across rough asphalt, so camera vibration arises from the wheel impacts and remains physically connected to the visible handle and her hands. She pushes with short, uneven steps beneath a narrow canyon of apartment buildings, which recede behind her. Let the rain remain soft and legible, not a foreground special-effects curtain. Maintain real scale, natural motion and continuous background parallax; no detached camera drift.

**Observed result.** The sampled low view shows the handle, both hands, feet and surrounding buildings. **Finding / revision.** The shot reused the idea of a cargo POV but changed the load and camera orientation after the depot. The major risk was breaking the physical link between cart, handle, person and camera; Blender attachment and a visible handle supplied that link. A later test added a very faint misty-rain layer to this export; see S12 weather variant.

## S13 — The return and the shopkeeper's call

Return-transition still · Fruit-shop still · Street-transition export · Fruit-shop return export · Saved revised prompt

**Production prompt.** Return to the same fruit shop and fixed S3 framing. The shop is closing but retains the earlier overcast daylight grade; the cleared cardboard area stays empty. From screen right, the grandmother pushes her mostly empty cart toward screen left **outside the railing**, on the road side, walking behind its handle. One folded printed board remains on the cart. The owner has already begun sweeping outside, inside the railing. Only when she reaches roughly the middle of the shop does he notice her and call, “阿婆！行得咁快啊，交完貨喇？” She slows gradually, stops without snapping into a pose, and looks toward him. He sweeps the cleared spot, says “……喂你等我一陣,” and walks back through the same shop entrance. The cart then stays still.

**Observed result.** `S13.mp4` is a wide return through the junction; `S13-2.mp4` shows the owner and grandmother at the fruit shop. **Finding / revision.** The original return sometimes put her ahead of the cart, stopped her too abruptly, or made the owner shout as soon as she appeared. The revised route placed her behind the cart and outside the rail, gave the owner an initial sweeping beat, and let her slow before stopping. A later variant added very faint misty rain to `S13.mp4`: weather test.

## S14 — The folded board and the fruit gift

Gift-action still · Combined 30-second working export · 15-second Blender blocking · Saved prompt variant

**Production prompt.** Continue the previous shot's **exact fixed wide frame**, light and person/cart locations. The cart stays parked for the entire interaction. The grandmother removes the single already-folded printed board from its platform, opens it along the existing crease without passing through her head or arms, and holds it above herself. The owner returns from the same shop doorway with one bag of fruit and thanks her for clearing the cardboard earlier. She politely refuses; he insists they should help one another and hooks the bag over the handle from his side of the railing. The bag has a continuous path from his hand, above the barrier, to the cart; neither person or object passes through the rail. Keep Cantonese dialogue natural and distant within the wide shot. No camera push-in for the package or bag. The source clips and compound generation must keep matching exposure, grade, crop and weather.

**Observed result.** The later sampled frames show the grandmother under the opened board and the owner reaching the bag toward the handle. **Finding / revision.** A single new generation changed composition, brightness and rain intensity across the S13/S14 join. A combined two-video generation reduced some disjunctions but could still carry unwanted rain from the source. The production subsequently tested direct rain reduction in S14. This is a concrete example of a limit of negative prompts: asking for “no rain” does not necessarily remove rain already baked into video references.

## S15 — A view from directly above

Still · Working export · Blender blocking

**Production prompt.** Lock the camera perfectly vertical above the fruit-shop awning and adjacent road. The weathered red canvas awning hides most of the owner. The grandmother is mostly obscured by the printed board she holds overhead; the cart, its mesh platform, and the fruit bag remain more visible. After her brief Cantonese acknowledgement, “嗯，好啊,” she moves slowly toward the bottom of frame, taking the cart with her. Maintain the screen positions of awning, railing and curb. No tilt, dolly, close-up, duplicate person or newly loaded paper.

**Observed result.** The top-view frame reads as a simple graphic: red awning at left, walkway and railing, then cart and printed board. **Finding / revision.** The board and awning both conceal people, so visibility had to be planned from directly above. The departing route was specified as down-frame instead of a vague “walk away.”

## S16 — Leaving with the fruit

Still · Working export · Final white-model route · Saved three-image prompt

**Production prompt.** Fixed full-wide return to the original Hong Kong intersection at the same scale as S2. Keep buildings and road dominant; the grandmother plus board occupies only about one tenth of the frame height in the middle distance. She travels steadily from screen right toward screen left, behind and pushing one four-wheel cart. Her **left hand** holds the open, previously folded printed board above her head; her **right hand stays on the cart handle** as she walks. A fruit bag hangs from the handle on her left side and swings lightly. There is no new paper stack. Her Cantonese line thanking the owner begins early, followed by his warm off-screen reply. Match the scene plate's light, softness and grain on skin, clothes, cart and bag. Do not enlarge her, add vehicles, leave the cart untouched, or use the white model's materials.

**Observed result.** The intersection export shows her and the cart crossing the wide street; the road and tall buildings retain most of the frame. **Finding / revision.** Earlier generations made the person and cart too large and too different in colour from the background, or failed to keep a hand on the handle. The final prompt separated hand roles, projected figure scale, and colour matching. The three-image setup used scene, wide-scale blocking, and pose references; the Blender white-model video was used to inspect movement, not necessarily uploaded in that final setup.

## What changed across the film

The recurring failure was **discontinuous physical ownership**: cardboard multiplied, the cart changed cargo or side, and scene fixtures moved to fill newly empty space. The recurring correction was an inventory and a single permitted transformation per shot. Camera scale was the second recurring issue. A fixed shot required explicit composition anchors, especially when the requested action involved small hands and props. The third issue was reference conflict: a previous video, a scene image, and a white-model test could each suggest a different camera or weather state. Giving each asset a limited responsibility made the most useful generations more repeatable.

These notes are an honest record of a hybrid production. Blender improved staging; still-image generation established identity and mood; Seedance supplied moving photographic performances; editorial repair and grading addressed some remaining seams and rain. None of the individual tools guaranteed continuity by itself.
